title: Inclusion Control on Mechanical Performance Optimization in G17CrMoV5-10 Heat-Resistant Cast Steel Through AOD Refining and Deoxidation Strategies
abstract: Abstract High-temperature Cr–Mo–V cast steels are widely used in applications above 540 °C, where microstructural stability and mechanical performance are critical. This study investigates the influence of casting route and deoxidation practice on inclusion characteristics, microstructure, and mechanical behavior of G17CrMoV5-10 cast steel. Quantitative analysis revealed a significant reduction in inclusion areal fraction from 0.751 to 0.031% (~96%), accompanied by a transformation from irregular multiphase inclusions to spherical Ca–Al–O-based morphologies. In addition, pronounced grain refinement ( G  = 11.65 → 14.54) and a more dispersed carbide distribution were observed, with carbide number density increasing from 745 to 1082 and average size decreasing from ~0.393 to ~0.240 µm 2  after AOD processing. These microstructural changes led to measurable improvements in mechanical properties. At room temperature, yield strength increased from 540 to 572 MPa and tensile strength from 661 to 684 MPa, while impact energy increased from ~87 J to ~125 J. At 550 °C, yield strength increased from 352 to 396 MPa and tensile strength from 394 to 442 MPa, while elongation decreased from 31.8 to 23.2%, indicating a strength–ductility trade-off. The results indicate that the observed improvements are governed by the combined effects of processing route, inclusion modification, grain refinement, and microstructural evolution, rather than a single dominant factor. This study provides a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of inclusion evolution, grain refinement, carbide distribution, and mechanical behavior at both room and elevated temperatures.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Inclusion control is closely related to the concept of clean steel, which is characterized by low levels of harmful impurities (such as oxygen, sulfur, phosphorus, hydrogen, and nitrogen) and nonmetallic inclusions. In addition, clean steel requires controlled inclusion composition, morphology, size, and distribution in both the liquid and solidified states. Therefore, inclusion control aims not only to minimize the harmful effects of inclusions, but also to achieve beneficial modification during steel processing. 1  Recent research on inclusion control focuses on optimizing refining conditions and processing routes, including slag composition, calcium treatment, and rare earth additions, to modify inclusion composition and morphology. 2  Metal casting enables complex geometries, compositional flexibility, and control over microstructure, making it suitable for high-temperature applications in industries such as automotive, chemical, and energy sectors. In such applications, alloy design is primarily guided by operating conditions. 3  To meet industrial demands for high performance, understanding the role of alloying elements is essential. Elements such as V, Cr, and Mo contribute to the unique properties of these alloys, enabling their use in demanding applications such as aerospace, energy, and automotive industries. 4  Cr–Mo and Cr–Mo–V cast steels are widely used in high-temperature applications such as steam turbines, valves, and petrochemical systems due to their balanced strength, creep resistance, and thermal stability. However, prolonged service under such conditions leads to microstructural degradation, which can reduce performance. Therefore, mechanical behavior in these steels depends not only on alloy composition but also on microstructural cleanliness, inclusion morphology, and carbide distribution. 5 ,  6 – 7  Chromium–molybdenum steels can be classified into low, intermediate, and high-alloy systems based on chromium and molybdenum content. This classification also includes Cr–Mo–V steels and various modified compositions. 8 ,  9  Chromium (Cr), molybdenum (Mo), and vanadium (V) play critical roles in determining the microstructure and high-temperature performance of these steels. Cr provides corrosion and oxidation resistance while increasing hardenability and strength at elevated temperatures. Mo improves toughness, crack resistance, and creep strength, and contributes to secondary hardening during tempering. Vanadium (V), as a strong carbide/nitride-forming element, inhibits grain growth and enhances strength through precipitation hardening, while also improving resistance to hydrogen attack. However, excessive V may lead to a slight reduction in ductility. Cr–Mo–V steels are typically produced by adding small amounts of V (≈0.2–0.3%) to Cr–Mo compositions, which significantly influences the microstructure. The formation of vanadium carbide (VC) phases at grain boundaries during hardening suppresses grain growth and lowers transformation temperatures, promoting bainitic/martensitic structures. As a result, Cr–Mo–V steels exhibit enhanced creep resistance, improved mechanical properties, and longer service life compared to conventional Cr–Mo steels. 10 ,  11 – 12  This study addresses two main aspects: (i) the relationship between microstructure and mechanical properties, evaluated through impact and tensile tests at both room and service temperatures, and (ii) the influence of deoxidation practice on inclusion morphology and distribution. Previous studies have shown that inclusion characteristics are strongly influenced by deoxidation practices and secondary metallurgical processes, including refining operations. 13 ,  14  These studies generally focus on improving steel cleanliness and controlling inclusion morphology through deoxidation and refining strategies. However, for Cr–Mo and Cr–Mo–V cast steels, the literature has predominantly addressed different aspects. Most studies examine single variables, such as alloying modifications, heat treatment conditions, or rare earth additions, in relation to microstructure and mechanical properties. In many cases, mechanical evaluation is limited to impact toughness, while other studies focus on microstructural evolution during long-term high-temperature service. 15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18  Studies addressing the combined influence of melting route, deoxidation strategy, and refining processes on inclusion evolution and mechanical behavior in these alloys remain limited. In this context, the present study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the relationship between processing conditions, inclusion evolution, and mechanical performance. Particular emphasis is placed on both room-temperature and elevated-temperature mechanical behavior. Unlike previous studies that primarily focus on single variables such as alloy composition, heat treatment, or impact toughness, the present study provides a combined quantitative evaluation of inclusion evolution, carbide distribution, grain refinement, and mechanical behavior at both room and elevated temperatures. This integrated approach enables a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between processing conditions and mechanical performance beyond conventional single-parameter analyses.

sections.heading: Materials and Methods
paragraphs: In this study, the microstructure and mechanical properties of G17CrMoV5-10 cast steel were investigated at room temperature and 550 °C by modifying the casting route and deoxidation practices. The molds were prepared using a chemically bonded sand system (alpha-set process), in which silica sand was used as the primary molding material, bonded with phenolic resin and cured using appropriate hardeners. Chromite sand was selectively applied in critical sections. Two different casting and deoxidation routes were employed. In the first route, melting was performed in an induction furnace using Fe–Si–Zr (ferrosilicon–zirconium), Ca–Si (calcium–silicon), and Al (aluminum) as deoxidizers. In the second route, the melt was processed by induction melting followed by argon–oxygen decarburization (AOD), where Ca–Si (calcium–silicon), Al (aluminum), and FeTi (ferrotitanium) were used as deoxidizers. The chemical compositions of the alloys are given in Table  1 . Table 1 Chemical Composition of the Alloys (wt.%) Material C Si Mn P S Cr Mo Ni Al V Fe IND 0.16 0.41 0.74 0.018 0.012 1.35 0.94 0.28 0.022 0.20 Balance IND+AOD 0.17 0.51 0.70 0.018 0.001 1.38 1.00 0.34 0.022 0.25 Balance

Both routes were carried out at a tapping temperature of 1595–1600 °C. The charge materials consisted of steel scrap (cold-rolled deep drawing steel, commonly referred to as DKP), recycled gating elements, and alloying additions. Deoxidation additions were applied per tonnage, with Fe–Si–Zr (0.098%), Ca–Si (0.098%), and Al (0.03%) in the induction route, and Al (0.67%), Ca–Si (0.04%), and FeTi (0.01%) in the AOD route. In the induction casting route, a low-density disposable ladle lining was used, consisting of 35–55 wt.% CaO, 40–45 wt.% SiO 2 , and 0–5 wt.% Al 2 O 3 . In the induction + AOD route, brick-lined crucibles containing 80–85 wt.% Al 2 O 3  were employed. The corresponding ladle configurations are shown in Figure  1 . Figure 1 Ladle configurations: (a) brick-lined ladle, (b) disposable ladle lining, and (c) exterior view.

The AOD refining process was conducted in two main stages. In the first stage (decarburization/refining), oxygen and inert gases (N 2  and Ar) were injected at an approximate O 2 /inert gas ratio of 3:1 with a total flow rate of ~8 m 3 /min. It should be noted that, prior to AOD processing, the melt composition was intentionally adjusted to a target range of 1.10–1.20 wt.% C and 0.90–1.00 wt.% Si in order to facilitate efficient decarburization and process stability during the initial refining stage. These values represent pre-AOD process targets rather than the final chemical composition of the alloy.

In the second stage (reduction/desulfurization), the gas ratio was adjusted to approximately 1:1 under similar flow conditions. A final mixing stage was applied prior to casting. All samples were subjected to identical heat treatment conditions. Austenitization was performed at 930 °C, followed by quenching in a polymer-based aqueous solution (15 wt.%), and tempering was carried out at 720 °C. The AOD process and its schematic representation are shown in Figure  2 . Figure 2 Argon–Oxygen decarburization (AOD) process: (a) industrial view and (b) schematic representation.

Test blocks were designed based on the final component geometry and modeled using Siemens NX (Figure  3 ). Specimens were sectioned, mounted, ground, polished, and initially etched with 4% Nital for metallographic analysis. Grain boundaries were revealed using an oxidation-assisted delineation method. Samples were heat treated at 855 ± 15 °C for 1 hour and air cooled, followed by grinding and polishing. Etching was then performed using a picric acid-based solution containing HCl and a surfactant at 80–90 °C for 5–7 seconds to clearly delineate grain boundaries. Grain size measurements were carried out using the planimetric method in accordance with ASTM E112. Microstructural and inclusion analyses were performed using optical microscopy and SEM–EDS. Figure 3 Test block geometry and corresponding cast specimens.

Mechanical properties were evaluated by tensile, Charpy impact, and Brinell hardness tests. Hardness measurements were performed using a 2.5-mm indenter under a load of 62.5 kg, and five measurements were averaged for each sample. Fracture surfaces were examined by SEM. High-temperature tensile tests at 550 °C were conducted in accordance with EN ISO 6892-1 (Method A1). A preload of 400 N was applied, and strain rates were set as follows: 0.005 min −1  for elastic modulus determination and yield point, and 0.05 min −1  for testing. All experiments were repeated, and statistical evaluation was performed using 90% confidence intervals.

sections.heading: Result and Discussion
paragraphs: Figure  4  presents the polished surfaces of samples produced by induction and induction + AOD routes. Residual features are indicated by arrows. Figure 4 Polished surfaces of samples: (a) induction and (b) induction + AOD conditions.

Optical observations (Figures  4 – 5 ) reveal clear differences in inclusion density, morphology, and spatial distribution between the processing routes. The induction condition is characterized by a higher density of irregular inclusions, whereas the induction + AOD condition exhibits fewer and more uniformly distributed inclusions. Figure 5 Higher magnification (20×) views of samples: (a) induction and (b) induction + AOD conditions.

Quantitative ImageJ analysis shows that the inclusion areal fraction decreased from 0.751 to 0.031%, corresponding to an approximate 96% reduction. This result indicates a significantly cleaner matrix in the AOD-processed condition. However, this improvement should not be attributed solely to the AOD process or deoxidation practice, but rather the combined effects of compositional differences, inclusion modification, and refining conditions. In particular, the reduced sulfur content and the presence of calcium during AOD processing contribute to the suppression of sulfide formation and the modification of oxide inclusions. The formation and evolution of nonmetallic inclusions are governed by deoxidation and refining practices. 19 ,  20  Aluminum-based deoxidation leads to the formation of Al 2 O 3  inclusions (2[Al] + 3[O] → Al 2 O 3 ), while silicon contributes to SiO 2  formation ([Si] + 2[O] →  SiO 2 ), often resulting in complex oxide structures. 14 ,  19  Zirconium additions may also promote the formation of stable ZrO 2  inclusions ([Zr] + 2[O] → ZrO 2 ), which can act as nucleation sites for multiphase inclusion development. 19  Calcium treatment modifies these inclusions into CaO–Al 2 O 3  phases (Ca + Al 2 O 3  → CaO–Al 2 O 3 ), resulting in more globular and deformable morphology. 14  In addition, exogenous inclusions originating from refractory-metal interactions may also contribute to the overall inclusion population. 19 ,  20  The proposed inclusion transformation mechanisms are also consistent with thermodynamic predictions reported in the literature. Accordingly, the induction condition is dominated by irregular and angular inclusions, whereas the AOD condition exhibits more spherical and chemically modified inclusions, consistent with calcium-driven inclusion modification under improved refining conditions. Sharp-edged, multiphase, and glassy-looking inclusions observed in the induction condition are consistent with ZrO 2 -core oxides surrounded by Mn–Si-based glassy phases reported in the literature. 21 ,  22  Following AOD processing, a clear tendency toward inclusion spheroidization and calcium aluminate formation is observed, which is associated with calcium-driven inclusion modification during refining. Due to the presence of Ti in the deoxidation practice, the formation of TiN or Ti(C, N)-type particles may also occur in localized regions. Previous studies indicate that coarse TiN particles can adversely affect toughness and fatigue behavior, whereas a finer and more dispersed distribution reduces this effect. 23 ,  24  These features will be further evaluated through SEM–EDS analyses in subsequent sections. The alloy was produced using a disposable ladle lining system during induction casting, which is generally associated with reduced refractory degradation and lower entrainment into the molten steel. Since refractory materials can act as a source of exogenous inclusions, their contribution should be considered in evaluating melt cleanliness. In the present study, the AOD-processed condition appears to exhibit a lower level of refractory-related inclusions, further contributing to improved microstructural cleanliness.

The microstructures etched with 4% Nital (Figure  6 ) reveal a ferrite–pearlite matrix with locally developed lath-type features. Grain boundaries are decorated with discontinuous carbide precipitates, consistent with Cr–Mo-rich M 23 C 6 -type carbides. In addition, fine intragranular features are observed, which are attributed to dispersed MX-type precipitates associated with vanadium. Figure 6 Etched microstructures at 100×: (a) induction and (b) induction + AOD conditions.

As shown in Figure  7 , clear differences in carbide morphology and distribution are observed between the processing routes. The induction condition exhibits relatively coarser and more locally clustered carbides, with partially continuous grain boundary networks. In contrast, the induction + AOD condition shows a finer, more uniformly distributed carbide structure with thinner and more discontinuous grain boundary carbides, indicating improved dispersion and microstructural homogeneity. The comparison presented in Figure  8  further highlights the transition from coarser and clustered carbides in the induction condition to a finer and more dispersed morphology in the AOD condition, supporting the observed differences in microstructural uniformity. Figure 7 Optical microstructures: (a) induction and (b) induction + AOD conditions. Figure 8 Microstructure comparison of (a) induction and (b) AOD conditions.

The micrographs used for quantitative carbide analysis are presented in Figure  9 . Quantitative image analysis was performed using ImageJ to evaluate carbide size and distribution, and the results are summarized in Table  2 . The induction condition exhibits a lower number density (745) and a larger average carbide size (~0.393 µm 2 ), indicating coarser and more clustered carbides. In contrast, the AOD condition shows a higher number density (1082) and a smaller average size (~0.240 µm 2 ), demonstrating a refined and more dispersed carbide distribution. The carbide area fraction remains similar in both conditions (~9–10%), indicating that the total carbide content is not significantly affected by the processing route. Figure 9 Representative micrographs used for quantitative carbide analysis: (a) induction and (b) induction + AOD conditions. Table 2 Quantitative Carbide Analysis Results Obtained Using ImageJ for Induction and AOD Conditions Condition Count Average Size (µm 2 ) Area fraction (%) IND 745 0.393 10.15 IND+AOD 1082 0.240 9.35

Grain size analysis was performed using the planimetric method on optical micrographs obtained from different regions of both induction and AOD samples to ensure representativeness. As shown in Figure  10 , both conditions are presented for direct comparison of grain morphology and grain size distribution. Figure 10 Grain size distribution obtained by the planimetric method for (a) induction ( G  = 11.65) and (b) AOD ( G  = 14.54) conditions.

A total of 100 grains were measured for each condition, providing statistical reliability. The average ASTM grain size number was determined as  G  = 11.65 for the induction condition and  G  = 14.54 for the AOD condition, indicating significant grain refinement after AOD processing. This increase in grain size number (Δ G  ≈ 2.9) corresponds to a reduction in effective grain size and a more refined microstructure. The observed grain refinement suggests that AOD processing contributes to microstructural evolution in addition to inclusion modification. However, this effect acts in conjunction with improved micro-cleanliness rather than as a sole controlling factor in the mechanical behavior. This combined effect is reflected in the mechanical properties, as discussed in the following section.

SEM images of the induction-cast sample (Figure  11 ) show angular, high-contrast inclusions dispersed within the matrix. At higher magnification, these inclusions exhibit irregular and sharp-edged morphologies. The corresponding EDS spectra (Figure  12 ) indicate that these inclusions are multiphase rather than compositionally uniform. Figure 11 SEM images of angular multiphase inclusions in the induction-cast sample at different magnifications. Figure 12 Representative EDS spectra of inclusions in the induction-cast sample.

Detailed SEM–EDS analysis reveals Zr-rich core regions associated with angular morphologies, where strong Zr and O peaks confirm the presence of ZrO 2 -type oxide phases. Surrounding these cores, additional Mn, Si, Ca, and Al signals indicate the formation of complex Mn–Si–Ca–Al–O oxide systems, consistent with the applied Fe–Si–Zr/Ca–Si/Al deoxidation practice. Minor S peaks suggest the presence of thin sulfide phases, such as MnS or CaS, while weak N signals indicate the possible formation of fine nitride or carbonitride phases (e.g., VN or V(C,N)), although these cannot be conclusively identified by EDS alone. A weak P signal may be associated with charge materials or refractory-related contributions.

From a morphological perspective, these inclusions exhibit heterogeneous and angular structures. The limited spheroidization of Zr-rich oxides, associated with their high melting temperature and poor wettability, may restrict their accommodation within the matrix and promote local stress concentration. Overall, the induction condition is characterized by multiphase oxide–oxy-sulfide inclusions consisting of Zr-rich cores surrounded by complex oxide phases.

SEM–EDS analyses of the AOD-treated sample (Figure  13 ) revealed a significantly reduced number of inclusions, predominantly exhibiting spherical, smooth-surfaced, and low-contrast morphologies. This transformation is associated with the modification of oxide inclusions into Ca–Al–O (calcium aluminate) phases under Ca–Si/Al/Ti deoxidation conditions during AOD processing. Figure 13 SEM images and corresponding EDS spectra showing spherical Ca–Al–O-based inclusions in the AOD-treated sample.

The dominant Ca, Al, and O peaks observed in the EDS spectra confirm the formation of Ca–Al–O–based oxides, while the presence of Si suggests the development of complex Ca–Al–Si–O inclusion compositions. Compared to the induction-cast condition, sulfide-related signals are significantly reduced, consistent with the lower sulfur content (~0.001 wt.%), indicating suppression of elongated MnS inclusions and stabilization of sulfur in the form of fine CaS phases associated with oxide inclusions. From a mechanistic perspective, calcium modifies solid alumina inclusions according to: [Ca] + Al 2 O 3  → CaO–Al 2 O 3  and stabilizes residual sulfur through: [Ca] + [S] → CaS. These reactions promote the transformation of solid Al 2 O 3  into low-melting calcium aluminate phases, reduce interfacial energy, and enhance inclusion spheroidization. The high fluidity of the molten metal during AOD processing further facilitates this transformation, resulting in more rounded and deformable inclusions. Although the MgO–CaO-based refractory lining used in the AOD process may introduce limited Mg and Ca into the melt, no significant Mg enrichment was detected in the present analyses, indicating that refractory contributions remain secondary. It should also be noted that the refractory systems differ between the processing routes. The induction furnace is typically lined with a neutral Al 2 O 3 -based refractory, whereas the AOD converter employs a basic dolomitic lining (CaO–MgO based). This difference in refractory chemistry may influence the type and composition of exogenous inclusions, particularly in terms of oxide stability and oxygen activity at the metal–refractory interface. In addition to deoxidation reactions, refractory-metal interactions may also contribute to inclusion formation. Interactions between molten steel and refractory oxides such as SiO 2  and Al 2 O 3  may lead to oxygen transfer and subsequent oxide inclusion formation. These interactions may contribute to the presence of exogenous inclusions observed in the microstructure. 19 ,  20

In the present study, the role of refractory-metal interaction differs between induction melting and AOD refining due to the use of different lining materials. Such interactions are widely reported in secondary steelmaking, particularly in relation to refractory dissolution and inclusion entrainment mechanisms. 25 ,  26  In the induction furnace, lined with a neutral Al 2 O 3 -based refractory, inclusion formation is predominantly governed by the applied Fe–Si–Zr/Ca–Si/Al deoxidation sequence. SEM–EDS analyses revealed Zr-rich oxide cores together with complex Mn–Si–Al–Ca–O phases, which are consistent with deoxidation products. Although refractory-metal interaction may occur through local dissolution or entrainment mechanisms, no distinct compositional evidence directly attributable to refractory-derived species was identified, indicating that its contribution remains secondary under the present conditions. In contrast, AOD processing results in a clear transformation in inclusion chemistry and morphology. Under these conditions, inclusion evolution is primarily controlled by modification reactions introduced via Ca–Si/Al/Ti additions. In addition to calcium-driven modification, titanium introduced during AOD processing may participate in inclusion and precipitation behavior due to its strong affinity for oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon, leading to the possible formation of TiO x , TiN, and Ti(C,N) phases. 27 ,  28 – 29  These phases are typically fine and dispersed and may contribute to inclusion modification or microstructural refinement, although they could not be conclusively identified by SEM–EDS analysis.

The formation of multiphase inclusions observed in this study can be rationalized based on established thermodynamic and kinetic principles governing deoxidation and inclusion modification in steel systems. 30 ,  31 – 32  In the induction melting route (Fe–Si–Zr 0.098%, Ca–Si 0.098%, Al 0.03%), aluminum deoxidation promotes Al 2 O 3  formation, while Si and Mn contribute to the development of complex Al–Si–Mn–O oxide systems. In addition, due to the strong oxygen affinity of zirconium, Zr-containing oxides form at early stages and act as heterogeneous nucleation sites, leading to locally ZrO 2 -rich regions. 30 ,  33  Under these conditions, the absence of effective modification mechanisms results in inclusions that remain irregular and angular. 31  In contrast, the AOD process (Al 0.67%, Ca–Si 0.04%, FeTi 0.01%) provides favorable thermodynamic and kinetic conditions for calcium activity, enabling the transformation of Al 2 O 3  into CaO–Al 2 O 3  phases. During subsequent cooling, sulfur enrichment promotes the formation of CaS in association with calcium aluminate inclusions, resulting in multiphase CaO–Al 2 O 3 –CaS structures. 32 ,  34  Thermodynamic considerations further indicate that inclusion evolution is governed by oxygen and sulfur activities, which control the transition from oxide to oxy-sulfide inclusions. 35 ,  36  Figure  14  shows a schematic illustration of the proposed inclusion evolution mechanisms in the induction and AOD processing routes. In the induction route, primary Al 2 O 3  inclusions interact with Si, Mn, and Zr, leading to the formation of complex Al 2 O 3 –SiO 2 –ZrO 2 –MnO inclusions with irregular morphology. In contrast, the AOD route is governed by Al–Ca–Ti interactions, where calcium modifies Al 2 O 3  into CaO–Al 2 O 3  phases, followed by CaS formation during cooling, resulting in multiphase oxy-sulfide inclusions with more spherical morphology. Figure 14 Schematic illustration of inclusion evolution in the induction and AOD processing routes.

Hardness measurements were used to evaluate the influence of microstructure and inclusion characteristics on the mechanical response. The induction-cast sample exhibited an average hardness of 202.2 ± 1.3 HB, whereas the induction + AOD condition showed a higher hardness of 228.2 ± 2.2 HB. Both conditions exhibited a ferrite–pearlite matrix with lath-type bainitic features associated with V-containing precipitates such as MX/VC/V(C,N). In the induction condition, sharp-edged ZrO 2 -rich oxide cores and multiphase inclusions may promote local stress concentration. In contrast, the AOD condition exhibits Ca–Al–O-based spherical inclusions and a more uniform distribution of bainitic laths, indicating improved matrix homogeneity. In addition, the AOD condition shows a finer and more uniformly distributed carbide structure together with significant grain refinement ( G  = 11.65 → 14.54), both of which contribute to increased resistance to deformation. The combined effects of inclusion modification, refined carbide distribution, and grain refinement are, therefore, consistent with the observed increase in hardness.

The results of the room-temperature tensile and Charpy impact tests are presented in Figure  15 . Tests were conducted in accordance with EN 6892-1 and ISO 148-1, and evaluated with respect to EN 10213 requirements. All measurements were performed on three specimens (n = 3), and results are reported as mean values with 90% confidence intervals. Figure 15 Tensile and impact test results of induction and AOD conditions; error bars represent 90% confidence intervals (n = 3).

In the induction-cast condition, yield strength and tensile strength were 540 ± 10 MPa and 661 ± 14 MPa, respectively, with elongation of 22 ± 1.7%, reduction of area of 61.8 ± 5.9%, and impact energy of 87 ± 8.5 J. Following AOD processing, yield strength and tensile strength increased to 572 ± 10 MPa and 684 ± 14 MPa, respectively, while elongation (24 ± 1.9%), reduction of area (69.4 ± 3.1%), and impact energy (125 ± 10 J) also improved. These improvements are associated with multiple microstructural factors. The modification of inclusions toward Ca–Al–O-based spherical oxides reduces stress concentration sites and enhances matrix compatibility. In addition, the AOD condition exhibits a finer and more uniformly distributed carbide structure, contributing to strengthening without promoting excessive local brittleness. Furthermore, grain refinement ( G  = 11.65 → 14.54) enhances strength through grain boundary strengthening mechanisms, while also supporting a more homogeneous deformation behavior. The combined effects of inclusion modification, carbide refinement, and grain size reduction therefore contribute to the observed improvements in both strength and ductility. Although compositional differences (particularly sulfur and vanadium content) may contribute to the observed variations, the consistent correlation between inclusion morphology, micro-cleanliness, carbide distribution, and mechanical response indicates that the processing route plays a significant role beyond composition alone.

The fracture surfaces of Charpy V-notch impact specimens were examined using SEM at magnifications of 200× and 600× (Figure  16 ). The micrographs reveal a mixed-mode fracture behavior characterized by the coexistence of ductile and brittle features. Brittle regions exhibit relatively flat, cleavage-like areas, while ductile regions show microvoid coalescence and dimple morphology. Figure 16 SEM images of fracture surfaces from Charpy impact tests at 200× and 600× magnifications: (a–b) induction and (c–d) induction + AOD conditions.

The induction-cast sample exhibits a heterogeneous fracture surface characterized by pits of varying sizes, coalesced microvoid regions, inclusion-related voids, and localized brittle features. This morphology is associated with microstructural heterogeneities, including sharp-edged ZrO 2 -rich inclusions, Mn–Si–O phases, and locally concentrated carbides, which promote stress concentration and early crack initiation. In addition, the non-uniform distribution of transformation products, including partially developed bainitic lath structures and carbide networks along grain boundaries, contributes to strain localization during deformation. These features are consistent with the relatively lower impact energy (~87 J) observed in the induction condition. In contrast, the AOD-processed sample exhibits a more homogeneous fracture surface with refined microstructural features. The ferrite–pearlite–bainite matrix shows a more uniform distribution, while carbide networks appear finer and more discontinuous. Furthermore, Ca–Al–O-based spherical inclusions improve matrix compatibility and reduce inclusion-related stress concentration sites. These changes are reflected in the fracture surface by a finer and more uniformly distributed dimple structure, fewer inclusion-related voids, and reduced large-scale microvoid coalescence, indicating a more dominant ductile fracture mechanism. This behavior is consistent with the increased impact energy (~125 J) observed in the induction + AOD condition. The statistical significance of the differences between the induction and induction + AOD conditions is summarized in Table  3 . A two-sample  t -test ( n  = 3) indicates that yield strength and tensile strength show statistically significant increases ( p  < 0.05), while impact energy exhibits a highly significant improvement ( p  < 0.01). In contrast, elongation and reduction of area show more limited variation and remain close to the statistical significance threshold. Overall, these results indicate that the applied processing route primarily enhances strength and toughness, with a comparatively smaller effect on ductility-related parameters. Table 3 Statistical Significance ( p -Values) of Mechanical Properties for the Induction and Induction + AOD Conditions Property p -value Yield strength (MPa) 0.005 Tensile strength (MPa) 0.015 Elongation (%) 0.047 Reduction area (%) 0.048 Impact energy (J) 0.0015

The high-temperature tensile results at 550 °C (Figure  17 ), evaluated with respect to EN 10213 requirements, deviate from the conventional relationship between ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and yield strength (YS) typically observed in ductile steels, indicating a temperature-dependent change in deformation behavior. At this temperature (≈0.4–0.45 Tm), thermally activated mechanisms such as dislocation climb and dynamic recovery become significant, modifying the balance between strength and ductility. In the induction-cast condition, the measured yield strength (352 MPa) and tensile strength (394 MPa) satisfy the target values and exhibit a relatively balanced strength–ductility response, with elongation of 31.8% and reduction of area of 84%, which can be associated with lower resistance to dislocation motion and more homogeneous plastic deformation. Following AOD processing, yield and tensile strengths increased to 396 MPa and 442 MPa, respectively, while elongation decreased to 23.2% and reduction of area remained nearly unchanged (≈83%), indicating a strength–ductility trade-off. This behavior is primarily related to differences in the distribution and effectiveness of microalloy precipitates. In the AOD condition, these precipitates are expected to be finer and more uniformly distributed, increasing resistance to dislocation motion even at elevated temperature. However, this also promotes earlier strain localization, leading to reduced elongation. In addition, improved micro-cleanliness reduces potential void nucleation sites; however, once void formation begins, the higher matrix strength promotes more localized void growth and coalescence. Overall, the observed behavior reflects the competition between precipitation strengthening and plastic deformation capability at elevated temperature. The statistical comparison of mechanical properties at 550 °C for the induction and induction + AOD conditions is presented in Table  4 . A two-sample t-test ( n  = 3) indicates that the increases in yield strength and tensile strength are statistically significant ( p  < 0.01). The change in elongation is also statistically significant ( p  < 0.01), whereas the reduction of area is not statistically significant ( p  > 0.05), suggesting that this parameter is relatively insensitive to the processing route under these conditions. Figure 17 High-temperature tensile properties at 550 °C for the induction and induction + AOD conditions. Table 4 Statistical Comparison ( p -Values) of Mechanical Properties at 550 °C for Induction and Induction + AOD Conditions Property p -value Yield strength (MPa) 0.0019 Tensile strength (MPa) 0.0018 Elongation (%) 0.0003 Reduction Area (%) 0.6213

High-temperature tensile fracture surfaces were examined by SEM, and representative images are presented in Figure  18 . Figure  18 (a)–(b) shows low-magnification images, while Figure  18 (c)–(d) presents higher magnification views for the induction and induction + AOD conditions tested at 550 °C. In the induction-cast condition, the fracture surface exhibits pronounced necking and a fibrous morphology characteristic of ductile fracture. At higher magnification, the surface is dominated by dimples formed through microvoid nucleation, growth, and coalescence. The relatively larger and more uniformly distributed dimples indicate more homogeneous plastic deformation, consistent with the higher elongation (31.8%) and reduction of area (84%). In contrast, the AOD-processed sample shows a more localized deformation pattern with sharper and more defined fracture regions. Although the dominant fracture mechanism remains ductile, the dimples are finer and more localized, indicating increased resistance to plastic deformation. This behavior is associated with a more refined and uniformly distributed precipitate structure, which increases resistance to dislocation motion at elevated temperature and promotes earlier strain localization. As a result, elongation decreases (23.2%) despite the higher strength observed in the AOD condition, while the reduction of area remains high (≈83%). Figure 18 Fracture surfaces of high-temperature tensile specimens tested at 550 °C: (a–b) induction and (c–d) induction + AOD conditions at low and high magnifications.

Overall, the fracture morphologies confirm that the reduction in ductility is not associated with casting-related porosity, but rather with microstructurally controlled deformation behavior. The transition from more homogeneous to localized plastic deformation explains the strength–ductility trade-off observed at elevated temperature. Importantly, no evidence of casting-related porosity or gas defects was observed in either condition. The observed features are associated with microvoid nucleation, growth, and coalescence, which are characteristic of ductile fracture rather than solidification-related defects. Therefore, the reduction in ductility is not related to porosity, but to deformation-controlled mechanisms governed by microstructural refinement and precipitation strengthening. This distinction is critical in interpreting the fracture behavior at elevated temperature.

These findings highlight the importance of evaluating inclusion evolution, carbide distribution, and grain refinement together, rather than as isolated parameters, for understanding the mechanical behavior of Cr–Mo–V cast steels.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study demonstrates that AOD refining combined with controlled Ca–Si/Al/Ti deoxidation significantly improves the microstructural quality and mechanical performance of Cr–Mo–V cast steels. Compared to the conventional induction route, AOD processing results in a cleaner and more homogeneous matrix through effective inclusion modification, carbide refinement, and grain size reduction.

The AOD route promotes the transformation of irregular oxide–sulfide inclusions into spherical Ca–Al–O and CaS phases, accompanied by a more refined and discontinuous carbide distribution and significant grain refinement ( G  = 11.65 → 14.54). These microstructural changes reduce stress concentration sites and improve deformation behavior.

At room temperature, both strength and ductility are improved, with notable increases in yield strength (540 → 572 MPa), tensile strength (661 → 684 MPa), elongation (22% → 24%), and impact energy (~87 → ~125 J). Hardness also increases from 202.2 to 228.2 HB.

At 550 °C, yield and tensile strengths further increase (352 → 396 MPa and 394 → 442 MPa), while elongation decreases (31.8% → 23.2%), indicating a strength–ductility trade-off. However, the reduction of area remains nearly unchanged, confirming that significant plastic deformation capability is retained at elevated temperature.

Overall, the observed improvements are governed by the combined effects of inclusion modification, carbide redistribution, and grain refinement, rather than a single processing parameter. These results demonstrate that AOD-assisted processing provides an effective route for enhancing microstructural uniformity and achieving a balanced combination of strength and toughness in high-temperature cast steel applications. In particular, this study demonstrates that a combined quantitative analysis of inclusion evolution, carbide distribution, and grain refinement at both room and elevated temperatures provides a more comprehensive understanding of mechanical behavior than conventional single-parameter approaches.
